title: Build a Triple by Taking Maxes
statement:
You get a list of triples, each [a, b, c], and a target triple. In one move you pick two different positions i and j and replace triples[j] with the position-by-position maximum:

[max(ai, aj), max(bi, bj), max(ci, cj)]

You may make any number of moves, including none. Return true if target can end up as one of the triples in the list, otherwise false.

examples.why: Merge [2, 7, 1] with [4, 2, 3] to get [4, 7, 3]. The last triple must be left out: its 5 and 6 are already above the target.
Every target value appears somewhere, but the only 3 comes packed with a 9. A max can never bring the 9 back down to 2, so that triple is unusable.
Merge the first and the third. Merging everything would pull in the 5 and overshoot.

hints: A merge can only make numbers bigger. What does that say about a triple that has some value above the target?
Such a triple can never take part: any result it touches is too big forever. Every other triple is safe. Is there any harm in merging all safe triples together?
No: merging safe triples keeps every position at or below the target. So merge all of them and check whether each position reaches its target value.

explain.intuition:
Whatever you build is the position-by-position max of some group of the original triples, and a max never goes down. So a triple with any value above the target poisons every result it touches. Throw those out.

Now the greedy step: merge all the remaining safe triples. Why that never hurts: each safe triple is at or below the target in every position, so adding one more safe triple to a group can only raise a position up to, never past, the target. If some group of safe triples hits the target, the group of all safe triples hits it too. So you never need to choose which safe triples to use. All that is left is to check that, for each of the three positions, some safe triple has exactly the target value there.
steps: Keep three flags, one per position, all false.
For each triple, skip it if any of its values is bigger than the target's value in that position.
Otherwise, for each position where it equals the target, set that flag.
Return true when all three flags are set.
pitfalls: Checking only that each target value appears somewhere. In example 2 the 3 exists, but only in a poisoned triple.
Merging every triple, safe or not. Example 3 overshoots that way.
Requiring one triple to match two positions at once. Different safe triples can supply different positions, as in example 1.

solutions.title: Try every group of triples
solutions.idea: Any result is the max of some non-empty group of triples. Try every group with a bitmask and compare its max to the target.

solutions.title: Merge every safe triple
solutions.idea: Drop triples with any value above the target. Merging all the rest never overshoots, so just check that together they hit every target value.

followups: Return the fewest triples you need to merge. Is that still easy?
The tuples now have length d instead of 3. What changes in the running time?
